one_liner: Rust crate for optimal 1-D k-means (Wang and Song's Ckmeans); 1.6-2.1x faster than the Ckmeans.1d.dp C++ code on an M2 Pro.
what_it_does: It splits a list of numbers into k groups with the least total within-group sum of squares, exactly (not heuristically), which is the problem Ckmeans.1d.dp solves for R and Python and the usual replacement for Jenks natural breaks in choropleth classing. The API is ckmeans(&data, k) returning one Vec per cluster, ckmeans_indices returning the sorted data plus inclusive index ranges, ckmeans_optimal choosing k in a range (default 1..=9) by BIC with per-cluster centre, size and withinss, and roundbreaks for rounded class breaks. It is not a drop-in for kmeans_1d_dp(): there are no per-value labels in input order and no weighted or L1 variants, and the same core is exposed through a C FFI (include/header.h, cdylib) and an npm WASM package.
how_it_is_fast: It fills the k x n dynamic-programming matrices with the divide-and-conquer optimisation, the same bounds as the C++ 'loglinear' fill: the optimal split is monotone in i and in k, so each cell searches only between neighbouring split points. Each cell's search is a single pass that computes the segment cost once per candidate, where the C++ two-pointer loop evaluates two candidates per step. Long ranges (16 or more candidates) keep four independent running minima so the loop vectorises, and the column loop is compiled per SIMD level and picked at run time with fearless_simd (AVX2 or SSE2 on x86-64, NEON on aarch64). The matrices are flat contiguous arrays, the divide-and-conquer stack is preallocated and reused, and the input is scaled by a power of two and shifted by its median before the f64 prefix sums are built.
when_to_use: Exact 1-D clustering or class breaks (choropleth bins, histogram binning, natural-breaks style classing) on f64 data from about 10^4 to 10^6 values with k up to a few dozen
Choosing the number of groups automatically: ckmeans_optimal's BIC picks the same k as the R package (Rust reports the negated BIC values)
Rust, C (FFI) or browser/Node (WASM) projects that want Ckmeans.1d.dp results without linking LGPL C++ or embedding R or Python
Replacing heuristic Jenks or iterative k-means in 1-D when you need a guaranteed optimum at comparable or lower cost
when_not_to_use: Large n times k: both DP matrices are dense k x n (an f64 and a usize per cell, 16 bytes), so 1,000,000 values at k = 50 need about 800 MB plus a sorted copy (derived from FlatMatrix::new)
When you need per-value labels in input order, weights, the L1 criterion or k above 255 (k is a u8): use Ckmeans.1d.dp, which offers weighted, L1 and L2Y variants
Multi-dimensional data: this is univariate only

If you are staying in R or Python: calling Ckmeans.1d.dp with method 'loglinear' instead of the default 'linear' (SMAWK) was up to 1.33x faster in this same table (Uniform(0,1000), k = 50), with no language switch
Projects that need upstream contributions accepted: issue #48 (2026-10-04) says the repo no longer accepts pull requests, and the Cargo badge says passively-maintained

integration.dependencies: fearless_simd 1.0, num-traits, libc, wasm-bindgen and js-sys (the last two are unconditional dependencies, and the wasm module is compiled on native targets as well); optional cbindgen for the C header
integration.platforms: any Rust target; run-time AVX2/SSE2 selection on x86-64, NEON on aarch64, scalar elsewhere; wasm32 through wasm-bindgen; C FFI cdylib on non-wasm targets
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The functions take a slice and allocate their own matrices with no global state (from the source), so concurrent calls are independent. The FFI entry point wraps the call in catch_unwind and reports errors through a CkmeansStatus out-parameter.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same objective, same clusters and same BIC-selected k as kmeans_1d_dp() for unweighted L2 input, but a different API: no input-order labels, BIC sign reversed, k limited to u8, and no weighted or L1 modes

gotchas: Rust does more dynamic-programming work than the C++ in the measured calls, and it still wins. The C++ fills only the final cell of the last column (EWL2_dynamic_prog.cpp sets imin = N-1 for q = K-1), while ckmeans' fill_matrices computes the whole last column although backtrack reads only its last entry. At k = 3 that is two full columns against one plus a cell. Two other C++ costs are implementation choices, not language effects: it sorts an index vector through a static-pointer comparator and then gathers, where Rust calls sort_unstable_by on the values, and it scatters per-value labels back to input order. Neither was timed separately.

The C++ baseline's ldouble is typedef'd to double in the vendored precision.h (Ckmeans.1d.dp 4.3.6, commit c960a53), and both sides shift by the median, so precision is matched. The only comparison table is one Criterion run on an Apple M2 Pro (NEON); the x86 AVX2 path was measured only against the crate's own 2.1.0 (CHANGELOG: 22 to 32 percent faster on an AMD EPYC), not against the C++.

Version history matters: before 2.1.0 (2026-10-01), ckmeans_optimal selected k_max for most inputs, and the selected k and BIC values changed in 2.1.0. Versions 2.0.0, 2.1.0 and 2.2.0 shipped on three consecutive days (2026-09-30 to 2026-10-02). The licence moved from MIT OR Apache-2.0 (up to 1.0.6) to BlueOak-1.0.0 (from 1.2.0).

Input edge cases: NaN returns NanError. Infinite values give a partition with no optimality guarantee and NaN BIC. A k above the number of distinct values is silently reduced. Integers above 2^53 lose precision in the cost computation. Very wide ranges can be sub-optimal by less than f64 resolution (README 'Numerical Limits').
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling does 1-D clustering; the systems-and-safety siblings (sorts, file tools, compilers) solve other problems, so the choice is only between this crate and the Ckmeans.1d.dp baseline itself.
verified_claims_summary: bench_cpp/benches/compare.rs (Criterion, seeded inputs, one full-suite run on an Apple M2 Pro) times ckmeans 2.2.0 built with rustc 1.99.0 (LTO, codegen-units 1) against the vendored Ckmeans.1d.dp 4.3.6 C++ built with Apple clang 17.0.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG. Both methods are measured: 'linear' (SMAWK, the R/Python default) and 'loglinear'. ckmeans_indices is 1.69x to 2.12x faster than the faster C++ method in every row, and ckmeans_optimal, which also does the BIC step, is 1.61x to 1.88x faster. BIC selection over k = 1..9 takes 26.7 ms against 50.9 ms at n = 110,000 (1.91x) and 263.1 ms against 510.2 ms at n = 1,000,000 (1.94x). All ratios are derived from page data.
